svg.aria-label: How to write சட்டை: 5 parts, ச, ட, ், ை, ட, one after another
svg.title: Writing சட்டை
svg.desc: 5 parts written one after another: ச, ட, ், ை, ட (tamil). The parts are in the order the hand writes them, which is not always the order they are typed: a vowel sign written to the left of its consonant comes before it. Each vowel sign is drawn on its own, without the consonant it attaches to. Each part has its own group of frames; frame N of a group shows movements 1 to N of that part, the movement being added drawn in ink over the finished part, whose outline is read from _fonts/NotoSansTamil-Static.ttf. Each part is drawn at its own scale from its own cited stroke order, so the strip does not show how large the parts are next to each other, how far apart they sit, or any join between them. Stroke order: ச: Sankaran Radhakrishnan, Tamil Script Learners Manual, Appendix I: Hand-movements, Frame 3, ச (University of Texas at Austin), p. 191 <https://sites.la.utexas.edu/tamilscript/files/2009/08/hw_lettersinstructions.pdf>; ட: Sankaran Radhakrishnan, Tamil Script Learners Manual, Appendix I: Hand-movements, Frame 1, ட (University of Texas at Austin), p. 190 <https://sites.la.utexas.edu/tamilscript/files/2009/08/hw_lettersinstructions.pdf>; ்: Abhinaya Rajarajan, Varai (Swift Student Challenge 2026), reference drawings recorded by hand for the 18 Tamil consonants with pulli, க் to ன் (repository commit 952294fa, no licence: facts only) <https://github.com/abhinayaRajarajan/varai>; ை: HP Labs India, Lipi Toolkit, Lipi Indic Character Recognizers 4.0, Tamil recognizer, class 43 (ை, ai sign): stored online-handwriting prototypes from native Tamil writers (MIT licence, 2012) <https://lipitk.sourceforge.net/lipi-reco.htm>; ட: Sankaran Radhakrishnan, Tamil Script Learners Manual, Appendix I: Hand-movements, Frame 1, ட (University of Texas at Austin), p. 190 <https://sites.la.utexas.edu/tamilscript/files/2009/08/hw_lettersinstructions.pdf>. Source notes on variation: ச: Frame 3 numbers three upper-frame movements and a fourth that turns around ச's lower-left bowl. Native writers draw the four movements as one continuous stroke, and this ductus follows them in order without lifting: movement 3 ends at the tip of the middle bar, so the pen comes back along the bar to the inner crossing before it turns around the bowl. In HP Labs India's online Tamil handwriting data (the LipiTk 4.0 Tamil isolated-character recognizer, trained on hpl-tamil-iso-char), 88% of the 176 stored prototypes of ச are a single pen-down stroke. Tamil handwriting varies by school; this is one attested order fitted to the bundled Noto Sans Tamil outline. ட: Frame 1 numbers ட's left descent and rightward foot as two joined movements, while Module 1 identifies the letter and teaches the usual top-to-bottom and left-to-right motion. Tamil handwriting varies by school; this is one attested continuous order fitted to the bundled Noto Sans Tamil outline. ்: One writer's recorded reference drawings, stored in the order they were drawn. In all 18 the consonant body is one stroke and the puḷḷi is a separate second stroke, made after the body is complete, so it costs one pen lift. Its centre sits above the body at 0.47 to 0.65 of the body's width (0.54 for க்). An earlier reading of Info-farmer's Writing Tamil animations of the consonants on Wikimedia Commons, which show each consonant with its puḷḷi, also places the dot after the body. Confidence is medium: one recorded writer, and only stroke count, order and the dot's bounding box were read; the dot is about 10 by 13 canvas units, too small to say which way the pen moved, so the short downward dab drawn here is not a claim. The path is fitted to the bundled Noto Sans Tamil disc, which the font centres at 0.43 to 0.60 of the consonant's width, a little left of where this writer put it. Handwriting varies by writer. ை: The recognizer stores native Tamil writers' tablet pen traces, each resampled to 60 points. 189 of the 190 stored prototypes of the ai sign are one pen-down stroke. All 189 turn clockwise: the pen starts on the left (181 of 189), circles the small left loop, arches over to the right, rises through the middle into the second arch, and comes down on the right, where 146 end. The traces are scaled to a square, so they fix the start, the direction and the pen lifts, not the proportions: the path is fitted to the bundled Noto Sans Tamil outline. Handwriting varies by writer. ட: Frame 1 numbers ட's left descent and rightward foot as two joined movements, while Module 1 identifies the letter and teaches the usual top-to-bottom and left-to-right motion. Tamil handwriting varies by school; this is one attested continuous order fitted to the bundled Noto Sans Tamil outline.
svg.text: How it is written — 5 parts, one after another
Part 1 of 5 — one unbroken stroke · 4 movements
Part 2 of 5 — one unbroken stroke · 2 movements
Part 4 of 5 — one unbroken stroke · 3 movements
Part 5 of 5 — one unbroken stroke · 2 movements
Part 1: stroke order after Sankaran Radhakrishnan, Tamil Script Learners Manual, Appendix I: Hand-movements, Frame 3, ச (University of Texas at Austin), p. 191
Parts 2 and 5: stroke order after Sankaran Radhakrishnan, Tamil Script Learners Manual, Appendix I: Hand-movements, Frame 1, ட (University of Texas at Austin), p. 190
Part 3: stroke order after Abhinaya Rajarajan, Varai (Swift Student Challenge 2026), reference drawings recorded by hand for the 18 Tamil consonants with pulli, க் to ன் (repository commit
Part 4: stroke order after HP Labs India, Lipi Toolkit, Lipi Indic Character Recognizers 4.0, Tamil recognizer, class 43 (ை, ai sign): stored online-handwriting prototypes from native
This order is attested, not standardised; the source records where it varies.
